patient.chief_complaint: Two years of worsening memory and confusion, with a sudden deterioration three months ago
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Bruno Cattaneo is an 80-year-old retired shipyard welder with polyvascular atherosclerosis — coronary bypass at 68, claudication, and a long smoking history — who attends with his wife for cognitive assessment. Her account is of a gradual decline over two years with an abrupt deterioration three months ago, when over a single morning he became confused about the date and about which flat he lived in, and stayed noticeably worse afterwards. There was no weakness or speech loss on that day. Since then he has needed help dressing in the correct order, has twice put his shoes on the wrong feet, and no longer recognises his own street from the car. He remembers people and conversations when reminded of the setting. He has never had a documented stroke. His blood pressure runs at 150-160 systolic. He has a right carotid bruit that has been noted in his notes for two years without further imaging. His pulse is regular, and inpatient telemetry during his bypass admission twelve years ago showed sinus rhythm throughout. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuations and no dream enactment.

mri.impression: Right hemispheric infarct burden — two cortical infarcts and an internal border-zone lesion — with asymmetric right-predominant white matter change, all downstream of a severe right internal carotid stenosis. The unilateral distribution and the haemodynamic border-zone pattern identify a large-artery rather than a cardioembolic mechanism.

No atrial fibrillation and no atrial ectopy, which together with a documented history of sinus rhythm lowers the probability of an occult cardioembolic source relative to the severe carotid disease found on ultrasound.

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia — multi-infarct type from severe symptomatic right internal carotid stenosis, with a haemodynamic (internal border-zone) component

differential.key_features: Would not produce a strictly unilateral distribution with an internal border-zone pattern, and the ECG shows sinus rhythm without atrial ectopy in a patient with documented sinus rhythm historically
Recall is cue-responsive, medial temporal lobes are preserved, and the visuospatial and apraxic deficits localise to the infarcted right parietal cortex
Fazekas 2 change is present but asymmetric and follows the stenosed side; the cortical and border-zone infarcts are the substrate
Apraxia is present but there is no alien limb, no myoclonus, no progressive asymmetric rigidity, and the deficits appeared abruptly
No fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Gradual two-year decline with an abrupt step three months ago, cue-responsive memory, visuospatial and apraxic complaints, in a patient with polyvascular atherosclerosis and an uninvestigated carotid bruit

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 19/30 with executive, attentional and visuospatial impairment, cue-responsive recall, and localising apraxic and topographical features

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded; LDL 88 mg/dL still above the polyvascular target and impaired glucose regulation identified

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Three chronic right hemispheric infarcts including an internal border-zone lesion, with asymmetric right-predominant white matter change — a strictly unilateral haemodynamic pattern downstream of the stenosed carotid

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation as the embolic source and for the left ventricular hypertrophy of chronic hypertension
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy and old inferior Q waves; no atrial fibrillation or ectopy, lowering the probability of a cardioembolic source

optimal_actions.action: Image the extracranial carotid arteries to establish whether a large-artery source accounts for the cortical infarcts
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Severe right internal carotid stenosis of 70-80% with a hypoechoic plaque, ipsilateral to the infarcts — a large-artery mechanism and a revascularisation question

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Right-hemisphere-weighted multi-domain profile with preserved recognition memory

optimal_actions.action: Obtain MR angiography of the head and neck for intracranial large-artery stenosis or dissection
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirms the right internal carotid stenosis and shows no tandem intracranial lesion, which is the information needed before any revascularisation decision

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Refer for carotid revascularisation assessment for a symptomatic 70-80% stenosis, intensify medical therapy toward an LDL below 55 mg/dL for polyvascular disease, avoid excessive blood-pressure lowering until the stenosis is treated given the border-zone infarction, and continue single antiplatelet therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Revascularisation assessment arranged for symptomatic severe stenosis, lipid target set for polyvascular disease, and blood-pressure strategy adapted to the haemodynamic mechanism

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

Every lesion lies in one hemisphere downstream of a severe ipsilateral carotid stenosis, with an internal border-zone pattern; a cardioembolic source would not produce a strictly unilateral haemodynamic distribution, and the ECG shows no atrial ectopy

The mechanism is established as large-artery: unilateral infarcts including a border-zone lesion downstream of a 70-80% ipsilateral stenosis. A structural cardiac source would not explain that distribution

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Investigate a carotid bruit in a patient with unilateral hemispheric infarcts rather than leaving it recorded and unimaged
Document the cognitive deficit with education-adjusted instruments and record the localising features
Exclude the reversible causes of cognitive impairment
Obtain brain MRI and note the laterality of the infarcts and the presence of a border-zone pattern
Quantify the carotid stenosis and confirm it with a second modality before revascularisation
Refer for revascularisation assessment while intensifying medical therapy
Recognise that aggressive blood-pressure lowering can worsen border-zone ischaemia until the stenosis is treated
contraindicated_actions: Do not lower blood pressure aggressively before treating a severe stenosis with an internal border-zone infarct pattern
Do not add anticoagulation: there is no embolic source and the mechanism is large-artery
Do not order prolonged rhythm monitoring or echocardiography when the distribution is strictly unilateral and haemodynamic
Do not attribute an abrupt cognitive step to progression of a degenerative disease
key_reasoning_points: Laterality is a mechanism argument: infarcts confined to one hemisphere downstream of a severe ipsilateral stenosis are large-artery, whereas cardioembolism scatters across territories and hemispheres
The internal border-zone (rosary-like) pattern in the centrum semiovale is a haemodynamic signature and changes the blood-pressure strategy — perfusion depends on the stenosis until it is treated
A carotid bruit recorded in the notes for two years and never imaged is the failure this case is built on
Apraxia and topographical disorientation localise to right parietal cortex, matching the largest infarct, and their abrupt onset dates the step
Polyvascular disease justifies an LDL target below 55 mg/dL, lower than the general secondary-prevention target

red_herrings.intended_effect: Read as diffuse small-vessel disease and used to diagnose the subcortical subtype
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The white matter change is right-predominant and follows the stenosed carotid — it is downstream hypoperfusion, not symmetrical small-vessel arteriopathy

red_herrings.data_point: Prior coronary bypass with inferior Q waves
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a cardioembolic mechanism from ischaemic heart disease and prompts echocardiography and monitoring
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ischaemic heart disease marks the patient as atherosclerotic but the strictly unilateral border-zone infarct pattern points to the carotid stenosis, and no arrhythmia has ever been documented

key_educational_points: Infarct laterality distinguishes large-artery from cardioembolic mechanisms
The internal border-zone pattern is haemodynamic and modifies the blood-pressure target until the stenosis is treated
A symptomatic 70-99% carotid stenosis is a revascularisation question, and cognitive symptoms count as the presentation
Polyvascular atherosclerosis carries a lower LDL target than uncomplicated secondary prevention
